anti_patterns: Treating sequencer soft-confirmations as final: triggering irreversible L1 actions on unproven L2 output instead of waiting for proof verification or buying finality from a liquidity provider
Choosing validium-style off-chain data availability silently: keeping state-diffs off L1 for cost reasons while marketing L1-grade forced exits, which are impossible without reconstruction data
Ignoring proof-generation latency in UX design: promising instant hard finality when proving takes minutes and batches only close when full, leaving users staring at pending withdrawals
Skipping the forced-inclusion path: leaving users dependent on the sequencer mempool so a censoring or halted sequencer freezes accounts with no L1 deposit escape hatch
Upgrading proving circuits casually: deploying new circuit releases without fresh audits and, for SNARK systems, ceremony handling, risking a soundness bug that lets invalid state roots verify

Assuming validity proofs imply privacy: publishing plaintext state-diffs for data availability while telling users transactions are 'zero-knowledge' — scaling proofs verify correctness but still reveal state changes unless privacy is explicitly designed in
avoid_when: Single-organization internal system with trusted parties where a database suffices
Hard real-time control requiring deterministic sub-second hard finality
Low transaction volume where prover operating cost exceeds the L1 gas saved
Workloads needing exotic EVM precompiles unsupported or punitively expensive in proving circuits
Permanent on-chain history required with no indexer or archiving plan, given blob pruning after ~18 days
benefits: L1-grade validity: every batched state transition is cryptographically proven, so operators cannot corrupt state or steal funds (unlike sidechains)
Fast cryptographic finality: exits execute once the L1 contract verifies the validity proof — no ~7-day fraud-challenge delay as in optimistic rollups

Throughput and fee reduction: thousands of transactions per batch with ~40-100x lower fees than L1, via signature omission and compression (account indices instead of 20-byte addresses save ~28 bytes each)
No watcher assumption: neither users nor third parties must stay online monitoring blocks to prevent fraud, unlike payment channels or optimistic rollups
Unconditional forced exit: on-chain data availability lets anyone reconstruct L2 state and withdraw even if sequencers stop cooperating (unlike Plasma)
Optional privacy foundation: the same proof machinery can be configured to hide inputs, since validity and zero-knowledge are separable circuit properties
best_practices: Publish batch data as EIP-4844 blobs, not calldata, and size batches against the blob fee market rather than assuming near-zero data costs persist
Expose finality honestly in UX: label soft confirmations vs proven L1 finality and quote proof-lag estimates per batch
Keep the L1 forced-inclusion queue tested end-to-end, including the full deposit-to-mint and withdrawal-to-finalize paths on every upgrade
Plan history retention explicitly: run indexers or archivers for reconstruction data before the ~18-day blob pruning window closes
Choose the zkEVM compatibility tier deliberately (Type 1-4): full equivalence costs more proving effort than a circuit-optimized VM
Monitor prover lag and proving cost per batch as first-class SLOs; alert when batches queue faster than proofs close
Roadmap sequencer decentralization (shared sequencing, leader rotation, MEV auctions) instead of treating single-operator sequencing as permanent
component_types: Sequencer: orders user transactions, executes them in the off-chain VM, and assembles batches with compressed state-diffs
Prover: compiles each batch into the proving circuit and generates the succinct SNARK/STARK validity proof (pre-state root, post-state root)
L1 Rollup Contract: stores canonical state roots and batch roots, tracks deposits, and promotes post-state roots only after proof acceptance
L1 Verifier Contract: checks validity proofs in constant time without re-executing transactions, including pre-state-root match
Data-Availability Publisher: posts compressed pubdata (state-diffs, L2-to-L1 message roots) as calldata or EIP-4844 blobs for state reconstruction
Off-chain VM / zkEVM: L2 execution environment maintaining accounts, balances, and contract state as a Merkle tree
Forced-Inclusion Queue: L1 entry point letting users push transactions directly when the sequencer censors or halts
L2-to-L1 Messenger: accumulates withdrawal/message Merkle roots so users can prove inclusion and finalize exits on L1
context: Ethereum L1 processes roughly 15-30 TPS with volatile gas fees, pricing out high-volume applications (payments, trading, gaming) while remaining the most secure and decentralized settlement layer. A ZK-rollup moves execution and state off-chain: a sequencer executes transactions in an off-chain VM, batches thousands of them, computes a new Merkle state root, and submits compressed state-diffs plus a succinct validity proof (SNARK or STARK) to L1 rollup and verifier contracts. The L1 contract verifies the proof in constant time without re-executing transactions; if the proof is valid and its pre-state root matches the stored canonical root, the post-state root becomes canonical. Use when you need L1-grade security with much higher throughput and fast cryptographic finality, and can tolerate prover cost, proof latency, and L1 data-bandwidth caps.
design_principles: Validity over optimism: prove every transition correct up front instead of assuming correctness and disputing later
Data availability is security: no reconstruction data on L1 means no forced exit — treat DA downgrades as security downgrades
Verify, do not re-execute: L1 checks succinct proofs in constant time and never replays the batch
Compress everything: indices over addresses, state-diffs over full transactions, blobs over calldata
Escape hatches first: forced inclusion and forced withdrawal paths must exist before mainnet, not after an incident
Bind proofs to committed state: always match the proof's pre-state root against the canonical root before promoting the post-state
name: zk-rollup
references: Vitalik Buterin et al., EIP-4844: Shard Blob Transactions, 2022 — https://github.com/ethereum/eips/blob/master/EIPS/eip-4844.md
technology_stack: ZK Stack / zkSync Era (Boojum prover, EraVM)
Proof systems: Groth16/PLONK SNARKs, FRI-based STARKs, recursive aggregation
EIP-4844 blob-carrying transactions for batch data availability
tradeoffs: Prover cost and latency: proof generation needs specialized hardware and takes minutes per batch, so hard L1 finality lags soft confirmations
Data-bandwidth-bound throughput: every batch must post reconstruction data; L1 blob capacity (EIP-4844 target ~0.375 MB/block) caps scaling until full danksharding
Ephemeral blobs: blob data is pruned after ~18 days, so long-term history and auditability need external indexers
Circuit complexity: proving circuits are hard to build, audit, and upgrade; SNARK systems may need trusted-setup ceremonies per circuit
EVM-compatibility tension: exact-equivalence zkEVMs cost more proving effort than circuit-optimized VMs, constraining opcode and precompile support
Sequencer centralization: production sequencers are typically single-operator, creating censorship and MEV exposure with only the L1 forced-inclusion queue as fallback
STARK proof size vs SNARK setup: transparent STARKs avoid ceremonies but post larger proofs with higher L1 verification gas
use_cases: High-volume token transfers and micropayments needing L1 security at sub-cent fees
Order-book and perpetuals DEXs settling CEX-scale trade volume on L2 with fast L1 exits
On-chain gaming with thousands of state updates per minute and player-owned assets
Mass NFT minting and airdrops where L1 gas per item is prohibitive
Payroll and mass disbursements batching thousands of payouts into one proven state update
Payments apps requiring withdrawals to L1 without multi-day challenge delays
